§1.1 — Linear Vector Fields and the Matrix Exponential

The ten problems below develop the theory of linear ordinary differential equations via the matrix exponential, establishing the exponential as a flow, exploring its algebraic structure, and computing it explicitly in geometric cases.

§1.1 · 1 Remark 2 — The Matrix Exponential as Flow

QUESTION
Prove Remark 2: for the linear vector field \(p \mapsto Xp\) on a finite-dimensional vector space \(E\), the trajectory through \(p \in E\) is \(\gamma_p(t) = \exp(tX)p\), and \(t \mapsto \exp(tX)\) is a one-parameter group.
Answer

Statement. For a linear vector field on \(E\) given by \(p \mapsto Xp\), define

\[ \exp(tX) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k X^k}{k!}. \]

Then \(\gamma_p(t) = \exp(tX)p\) is the unique solution of \(\gamma'(t) = X\gamma(t)\), \(\gamma(0) = p\), and

\[ \exp((s+t)X) = \exp(sX)\exp(tX), \qquad \exp(0) = I. \]

Proof — Differentiation. Term-by-term differentiation of the series gives

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\exp(tX) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{kt^{k-1}X^k}{k!} = X\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^j X^j}{j!} = X\exp(tX). \]

Therefore \(\frac{d}{dt}(\exp(tX)p) = X\exp(tX)p\), confirming that \(\gamma_p(t) = \exp(tX)p\) solves \(\gamma'(t) = X\gamma(t)\), \(\gamma(0) = p\).

Proof — Group property. Since \(sX\) and \(tX\) commute, the formal exponential addition law applies:

\[ \exp(sX)\exp(tX) = \exp((s+t)X). \]

At \(s = t = 0\), \(\exp(0) = I\). Thus \(t \mapsto \exp(tX)\) is a one-parameter group of linear transformations.

KEY RESULT
The matrix exponential converts an infinitesimal linear generator \(X\) into the finite flow \(t \mapsto \exp(tX)\). The trajectory through \(p\) is \(\gamma_p(t) = \exp(tX)p\).

§1.1 · 2 Hyperbolic Case — cosh and sinh Decomposition

QUESTION
Verify \(\exp(X) = \cosh\lambda\, I + \tfrac{\sinh\lambda}{\lambda}X\) for the hyperbolic case \(X^2 = \lambda^2 I\), \(\lambda \neq 0\), using (a) power series, (b) diagonalization.
Answer

Setup. In the hyperbolic case, \(X\) is a traceless \(2{\times}2\) matrix with real eigenvalues \(\pm\lambda\), satisfying \(X^2 = \lambda^2 I\). The claim is

\[ \exp(tX) = \cosh(t\lambda)\,I + \frac{\sinh(t\lambda)}{\lambda}\,X. \]

(a) Power series proof. Since \(X^2 = \lambda^2 I\), powers reduce:

\[ X^{2k} = \lambda^{2k}I, \qquad X^{2k+1} = \lambda^{2k}X. \]

Splitting the exponential series into even and odd powers:

\[ \exp(X) = \underbrace{\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{2k}}{(2k)!}\right)}_{\cosh\lambda}\!I + \underbrace{\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{2k}}{(2k+1)!}\right)}_{\sinh\lambda/\lambda}\!X = \cosh\lambda\,I + \frac{\sinh\lambda}{\lambda}\,X. \]

(b) Diagonalization proof. Since eigenvalues \(\pm\lambda\) are distinct, write \(X = P\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,-\lambda)\,P^{-1}\). Then

\[ \exp(X) = P\begin{bmatrix}e^\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-\lambda}\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}. \]

One checks directly that \(\cosh\lambda\,I + \frac{\sinh\lambda}{\lambda}\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,-\lambda) = \mathrm{diag}(e^\lambda,e^{-\lambda})\), and conjugation by \(P\) gives the result.

KEY RESULT
When \(X^2 = \lambda^2 I\): \(\quad\exp(tX) = \cosh(t\lambda)\,I + \dfrac{\sinh(t\lambda)}{\lambda}\,X.\) The algebraic relation \(X^2 = \lambda^2 I\) causes the series to collapse into two hyperbolic functions, one for each parity of powers.

§1.1 · 3 Orthogonal and Unitary Exponentials — Skew-Symmetry

QUESTION
Show that \(\exp(\tau X)\) is orthogonal (resp. unitary) for all \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\) if and only if \(X\) is skew-symmetric (resp. skew-Hermitian).
Answer

Real (orthogonal) case. We use the identity \(\exp(\tau X)^T = \exp(\tau X^T)\).

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(\exp(\tau X)^T\exp(\tau X) = I\) for all \(\tau\). Then \(\exp(\tau X^T)\exp(\tau X) = I\). Differentiating at \(\tau = 0\):

\[ X^T + X = 0 \implies X^T = -X. \]

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(X^T = -X\). Then

\[ \exp(\tau X)^T\exp(\tau X) = \exp(\tau X^T)\exp(\tau X) = \exp(-\tau X)\exp(\tau X) = I. \]

Complex (unitary) case. Identical with \(T\) replaced by \(*\). We get \(\exp(\tau X)\) is unitary for all \(\tau\) iff \(X^* = -X\) (skew-Hermitian).

KEY RESULT
\(\exp(\tau X) \in O(n)\) for all \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\) \(\iff\) \(X^T = -X.\quad\) \(\exp(\tau X) \in U(n)\) for all \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\) \(\iff\) \(X^* = -X.\) This is the infinitesimal characterization of orthogonal/unitary groups: they are generated by skew-symmetric/skew-Hermitian matrices.

§1.1 · 4 Cross Product Vector Field in ℝ³ — Rodrigues' Rotation Formula

QUESTION
Let \(E = \mathbb{R}^3\), \(0 \neq x \in E\), and let \(X(p) = x \times p\).
(a) Choosing a right-handed ONB \((e_1,e_2,e_3)\) with \(e_3 \parallel x\), compute \(\exp(X)e_i\).
(b) Derive Rodrigues' formula: \(\exp(X) = I + \tfrac{\sin\|x\|}{\|x\|}X + \tfrac{1-\cos\|x\|}{\|x\|^2}X^2.\)
Answer

Part (a). Set \(e_3 = x/\|x\|\) and complete to a right-handed ONB. Since \(x = \|x\|e_3\):

\[ Xe_1 = x \times e_1 = \|x\|e_2, \quad Xe_2 = x \times e_2 = -\|x\|e_1, \quad Xe_3 = 0. \]

In this basis, \(X\) has the block form \(\begin{pmatrix}0 & -\|x\| & 0\\ \|x\| & 0 & 0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\). The upper-left block is a skew-symmetric infinitesimal rotation, whose exponential is a rotation by angle \(\|x\|\):

\[ \exp(X)e_1 = \cos\|x\|\,e_1 + \sin\|x\|\,e_2, \quad \exp(X)e_2 = -\sin\|x\|\,e_1 + \cos\|x\|\,e_2, \quad \exp(X)e_3 = e_3. \]

Part (b) — Rodrigues' Formula. Let \(a = \|x\|\). From the basis computation, \(X^2 = -a^2\) on the plane perpendicular to \(x\) and \(X^2 = 0\) along \(x\). Furthermore \(X^3 = -a^2 X\). Collecting odd and even powers separately from the series \(\exp(X) = I + X + X^2/2! + \cdots\):

\[ \text{Odd:}\quad X - \frac{a^2 X}{3!} + \frac{a^4 X}{5!} - \cdots = \frac{\sin a}{a}X. \] \[ \text{Even (beyond }I\text{):}\quad \frac{X^2}{2!} - \frac{a^2 X^2}{4!} + \cdots = \frac{1-\cos a}{a^2}X^2. \]
KEY RESULT — RODRIGUES' FORMULA
\[\exp(X) = I + \frac{\sin\|x\|}{\|x\|}X + \frac{1-\cos\|x\|}{\|x\|^2}X^2.\] This is the explicit formula for rotation in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) by angle \(\|x\|\) around the axis \(x\). The three terms represent: the fixed component along \(x\), the sine rotation, and the cosine correction.

§1.1 · 5 Exponential of a Jordan Block

QUESTION
Show that the exponential of the \(n \times n\) Jordan block \(J\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the matrix with \(e^\lambda / k!\) on the \(k\)-th superdiagonal.
Answer

Decomposition. Write \(J = \lambda I + N\), where \(N\) is the strictly upper-triangular matrix with 1's on the first superdiagonal. Note that \(\lambda I\) commutes with \(N\) and \(N^n = 0\) (nilpotency). Therefore

\[ \exp(J) = \exp(\lambda I)\exp(N) = e^\lambda\exp(N). \]

Since \(N^n = 0\), the exponential of \(N\) is a finite sum:

\[ \exp(N) = I + N + \frac{N^2}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{N^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}. \]

The matrix \(N^k\) has 1's exactly on the \(k\)-th superdiagonal. Therefore \(\exp(N)\) has \(1/k!\) on the \(k\)-th superdiagonal, giving

\[ \boxed{\exp(J) = e^\lambda\!\left(I + N + \frac{N^2}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{N^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\right).} \]
KEY RESULT
For a Jordan block \(J = \lambda I + N\) (\(N\) nilpotent, \(N^n = 0\)), the exponential \(\exp(J)\) has \(e^\lambda/k!\) on the \(k\)-th superdiagonal. The decomposition \(J = \lambda I + N\) into commuting summands — one scalar, one nilpotent — is the key algebraic step.

§1.1 · 6 Exponential of the Derivative Operator

QUESTION
Let \(E\) be the space of polynomials of degree \(\le n{-}1\), and let \(D = d/d\xi\). Show that \(\exp(\tau D)f(\xi) = f(\xi+\tau)\).
Answer

Proof. Since \(\deg f \le n-1\), we have \(D^n f = 0\). The series terminates:

\[ \exp(\tau D)f = f + \tau f' + \frac{\tau^2}{2!}f'' + \cdots + \frac{\tau^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}f^{(n-1)}. \]

By Taylor's theorem for polynomials, this is exactly

\[ f(\xi+\tau) = f(\xi) + \tau f'(\xi) + \frac{\tau^2}{2!}f''(\xi) + \cdots \]

Therefore \(\exp(\tau D)f(\xi) = f(\xi+\tau)\). The translation operator on polynomials is the exponential of differentiation.

Connection to Problem 5. In the basis \(\{1, \xi, \xi^2/2!, \ldots, \xi^{n-1}/(n-1)!\}\), the matrix of \(D\) is a nilpotent Jordan-type matrix with 1's on one off-diagonal — exactly the nilpotent part \(N\) of a Jordan block. Its exponential produces binomial/Taylor shift coefficients, mirroring the \(N\)-part of \(\exp(J)\).

KEY RESULT
\(\exp(\tau D)f(\xi) = f(\xi+\tau).\) The exponential of the differentiation operator is translation. This is a functional-analytic instance of the Jordan block exponential, with the shift appearing as the finite Taylor series.

§1.1 · 7 A Real Matrix That Is Not a Real Exponential

QUESTION
Show that \(A = \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is not the exponential of any real \(2{\times}2\) matrix.
Answer

Proof by contradiction. Suppose \(A = e^X\) for some real \(X \in M_2(\mathbb{R})\).

Step 1: Eigenvalue constraint. The only eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(-1\). If \(\mu\) is an eigenvalue of \(X\), then \(e^\mu\) is an eigenvalue of \(e^X = A\), so \(e^\mu = -1\), giving \(\mu = (2k+1)\pi i\) for some integer \(k\).

Step 2: Reality forces distinct eigenvalues. Since \(X\) is real, complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. The only option is \(\mu_1 = (2k+1)\pi i\) and \(\mu_2 = -(2k+1)\pi i\) — which are distinct. So \(X\) must be diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\), and is similar to \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-\theta\\\theta&0\end{pmatrix}\) with \(\theta = (2k+1)\pi\).

Step 3: Contradiction. The exponential of such a matrix is

\[ e^X = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} = -I. \]

But \(-I\) is diagonalizable, while \(A\) is not (it is a non-trivial Jordan block). Contradiction.

KEY RESULT
The matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is not in the image of \(\exp: M_2(\mathbb{R}) \to M_2(\mathbb{R})\). The obstruction is topological/algebraic: any real \(X\) with \(e^X = -I\) must produce a diagonalizable matrix, but \(A\) is not diagonalizable.

§1.1 · 8 Affine Transformations and Affine Vector Fields

QUESTION
Embed \(E\) as \(E^+ = \{(p,1)\} \subset E \times \mathbb{R}\). Show (a) affine maps \(p \mapsto ap+b\) are represented by \(\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\), and (b) the affine flow generated by \(p \mapsto Xp+v\) is \(p \mapsto \exp(\tau X)p + \tfrac{\exp(\tau X)-I}{X}v\).
Answer

Part (a). Identify \(p \in E\) with \((p,1) \in E^+\). Direct computation:

\[ \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}ap+b\\1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Similarly, the vector field \(p \mapsto Xp+v\) corresponds to \(\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}X&v\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\) since

\[ \begin{pmatrix}X&v\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}Xp+v\\0\end{pmatrix}, \]

which is tangent to \(E^+\) (last coordinate 0 = constant in \(\tau\)).

Part (b). Let \(B = \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}X&v\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\). Computing powers: \(B^k = \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}X^k & X^{k-1}v\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\) for \(k \ge 1\). Summing the series:

\[ \exp(\tau B) = \begin{pmatrix}\exp(\tau X) & \displaystyle\left(\tau I + \frac{\tau^2}{2!}X + \frac{\tau^3}{3!}X^2+\cdots\right)v\\[4pt] 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\exp(\tau X) & \dfrac{\exp(\tau X)-I}{X}\,v\\[4pt]0&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

The notation \(\tfrac{\exp(\tau X)-I}{X}\) means the power series \(\tau I + \tfrac{\tau^2}{2}X + \cdots\), valid even if \(X\) is singular. Equivalently, \(\tfrac{\exp(\tau X)-I}{X}v = \int_0^\tau \exp(sX)v\,ds\).

KEY RESULT
\[\exp(\tau A) : p \mapsto \exp(\tau X)p + \frac{\exp(\tau X)-I}{X}\,v = \exp(\tau X)p + \int_0^\tau \exp(sX)v\,ds.\] By embedding \(E \hookrightarrow E \times \mathbb{R}\), every affine problem reduces to a linear one in one dimension higher. This is a recurring technique in Lie theory.

§1.1 · 9 Trajectories of a Linear Vector Field

QUESTION
Let \(X \in M\). Show: (a) there is exactly one trajectory of \(X\) through each point; (b) if \(a \in GL(E)\) commutes with \(X\), then \(x \mapsto ax\) permutes the trajectories.
Answer

Part (a) — Existence and Uniqueness. The curve \(p(t) = \exp(tX)p_0\) satisfies \(p'(t) = Xp(t)\) and \(p(0) = p_0\) (existence). For uniqueness, if \(q(t)\) is another solution, define \(r(t) = \exp(-tX)q(t)\). Then

\[ r'(t) = -X\exp(-tX)q(t) + \exp(-tX)q'(t) = \exp(-tX)\bigl(-Xq(t) + Xq(t)\bigr) = 0. \]

So \(r(t)\) is constant, \(r(t) = r(0) = p_0\), hence \(q(t) = \exp(tX)p_0\).

Part (b) — Permutation by commuting maps. Suppose \(aX = Xa\). Since \(a\) commutes with \(X\), it commutes with every power of \(X\), hence with \(\exp(tX)\):

\[ a\exp(tX) = \exp(tX)a. \]

Therefore \(a\,p(t) = a\exp(tX)p_0 = \exp(tX)(ap_0)\), which is the trajectory through \(ap_0\). So \(a\) maps the trajectory through \(p_0\) to the trajectory through \(ap_0\).

KEY RESULT
The ODE \(\gamma' = X\gamma\), \(\gamma(0) = p_0\) has unique solution \(\gamma(t) = \exp(tX)p_0\). Any invertible \(a\) commuting with \(X\) is a symmetry of the vector field, permuting trajectories.

§1.1 · 10 Stationary Points and Limits of Flows

QUESTION
Show: (a) \(\exp(\tau X)p = p\) for all \(\tau\) \(\iff\) \(Xp = 0\). (b) If \(\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\exp(\tau X)p_0 = p_\infty\), then \(Xp_\infty = 0\).
Answer

Part (a). (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(\exp(\tau X)p = p\) for all \(\tau\), differentiate at \(\tau = 0\): \(Xp = 0\). (\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(Xp = 0\), then \(X^k p = 0\) for all \(k \ge 1\), so \(\exp(\tau X)p = Ip = p\).

Part (b). For any fixed \(s \in \mathbb{R}\), use continuity of \(\exp(sX)\) and the group property:

\[ \exp(sX)p_\infty = \exp(sX)\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\exp(\tau X)p_0 = \lim_{\tau\to\infty}\exp((s+\tau)X)p_0 = p_\infty, \]

since \(s + \tau \to \infty\) as \(\tau \to \infty\). By part (a), \(Xp_\infty = 0\).

KEY RESULT
Stationary ↔ in kernel. A point \(p\) is stationary under the flow \(\exp(\tau X)\) if and only if \(p \in \ker X\). Moreover, any flow limit is automatically a stationary point — a topological stability fact.

§1.2 — Properties of the Matrix Exponential

These thirteen problems develop the algebraic structure of the exponential map: how it interacts with nilpotent/semisimple decompositions, surjectivity onto invertible matrices, limit formulas, the Lie bracket, one-parameter subgroups, and invariant subspaces.

§1.2 · 1 Nilpotent ↔ Unipotent — A Bijection via the Exponential

QUESTION
Show that \(X \mapsto \exp X\) maps nilpotent matrices bijectively onto unipotent matrices, with inverse \(a \mapsto \log a\).
Answer

Nilpotent → Unipotent. Let \(X^k = 0\). The series terminates: \(\exp X = I + X + \cdots + X^{k-1}/(k-1)!\,=: I + N.\) Then \(N\) is a polynomial in \(X\) with zero constant term, hence nilpotent. Therefore \((\exp X - I)^m = N^m = 0\) for some \(m\), so \(\exp X\) is unipotent.

Unipotent → Nilpotent via log. Let \(a = I + N\) with \(N^k = 0\). Define

\[ \log a = \log(I+N) = N - \frac{N^2}{2} + \frac{N^3}{3} - \cdots \]

The series terminates since \(N^k = 0\). The result is nilpotent (polynomial in \(N\) with zero constant term).

Bijection. The formal power series identities \(\exp(\log(1+z)) = 1+z\) and \(\log(\exp z) = z\) hold as polynomials when \(N\) is nilpotent, confirming \(\exp\) and \(\log\) are mutually inverse.

KEY RESULT
\(\exp\) and \(\log\) restrict to mutually inverse bijections: \[\{\text{nilpotent matrices}\} \;\xleftrightarrow[\log]{\exp}\; \{\text{unipotent matrices}\}.\] Both series are finite when restricted to this domain, making the bijection algebraic (no convergence needed beyond nilpotency).

§1.2 · 2 Semisimple Matrices and the Exponential

QUESTION
Show: (a) exp maps semisimple matrices to semisimple matrices. (b) Every invertible semisimple matrix is an exponential of a semisimple matrix. (c) Characterize when two semisimple matrices have the same exponential.
Answer

Part (a). Let \(X = PDP^{-1}\) with \(D = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\). Then \(\exp X = P\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{\lambda_1},\ldots,e^{\lambda_n})\,P^{-1}\) is diagonal in the same basis, hence semisimple.

Part (b). Let \(a = PDP^{-1}\) be invertible semisimple, \(D = \mathrm{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)\) with \(\mu_j \neq 0\). Choose logarithms \(\lambda_j\) with \(e^{\lambda_j} = \mu_j\), using the same branch for equal \(\mu_j\). Set \(X = P\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\,P^{-1}\). Then \(X\) is semisimple and \(\exp X = a\). Moreover the \(\lambda_j\) can be chosen so no two distinct eigenvalues of \(X\) differ by a nonzero multiple of \(2\pi i\).

Part (c). If \(X, X'\) are both semisimple with the \(2\pi i\) separation condition (no two distinct eigenvalues differing by \(2\pi i k\)) and \(\exp X = \exp X'\), then \(X\) and \(X'\) have the same eigenspaces. Being simultaneously diagonalizable, their eigenvalues satisfy \(\lambda_j' - \lambda_j \in 2\pi i \mathbb{Z}\), i.e., \(-iX\) and \(-iX'\) have diagonals differing by multiples of \(2\pi\).

KEY RESULT
Semisimplicity is preserved by \(\exp\). Every invertible semisimple matrix is an exponential. The ambiguity in the semisimple logarithm is exactly the \(2\pi i\mathbb{Z}\) freedom in choosing the branch of log for each eigenvalue.

§1.2 · 3 Jordan Decomposition and the Exponential

QUESTION
Show: (a) Every invertible \(a\) writes uniquely as \(a = bc\) with \(b\) semisimple, \(c\) unipotent, \(bc=cb\). (b) If \(X = Y+Z\) is the (additive) Jordan decomposition, then \(\exp X = \exp Y \cdot \exp Z\) is the multiplicative Jordan decomposition.
Answer

Part (a) — Multiplicative Jordan decomposition. For invertible \(a\), write \(a = b + n\) (additive Jordan, \(b\) semisimple, \(n\) nilpotent, commuting). Since \(a\) is invertible, \(b\) is invertible. Set \(c = b^{-1}a = I + b^{-1}n\). Then \(b^{-1}n\) is nilpotent, so \(c\) is unipotent, \(a = bc\), and \(bc = cb\). Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of the additive Jordan decomposition. Both \(b\) and \(c\) are polynomials in \(a\).

Part (b) — Exponential intertwines decompositions. If \(X = Y + Z\) (semisimple \(Y\), nilpotent \(Z\), \(YZ = ZY\)), then \(\exp X = \exp(Y+Z) = \exp Y\exp Z\). By Problems 1 and 2, \(\exp Y\) is semisimple and \(\exp Z\) is unipotent and they commute. This is exactly the multiplicative Jordan decomposition of \(\exp X\).

Part (c) — Uniqueness criterion. Under the \(2\pi i\) separation condition on eigenvalues of \(X\): \(\exp X = \exp X'\) iff \(Z = Z'\) (nilpotent parts agree) and \(Y, Y'\) are simultaneously diagonalizable with eigenvalue differences in \(2\pi i\mathbb{Z}\). The nilpotent part is completely rigid; only the semisimple logarithm has the branch ambiguity.

KEY RESULT
\(\exp(Y + Z) = \exp(Y)\cdot\exp(Z)\) converts the additive Jordan decomposition \(X = Y + Z\) into the multiplicative decomposition \(\exp(X) = \exp(Y)\cdot\exp(Z)\), mapping semisimple to semisimple and nilpotent to unipotent.

§1.2 · 4 Every Invertible Complex Matrix Is an Exponential

QUESTION
Show that every Jordan block \(J\) with \(\lambda \neq 0\) is a complex exponential, and deduce that every invertible complex matrix is an exponential.
Answer

Jordan block. Write \(J = \lambda I + N\) with \(N\) nilpotent. Since \(\lambda \neq 0\), choose \(\mu \in \mathbb{C}\) with \(e^\mu = \lambda\). The matrix \(\lambda^{-1}N\) is nilpotent, so \(\log(I + \lambda^{-1}N)\) is a finite sum. Define

\[ X = \mu I + \log(I + \lambda^{-1}N). \]

Since \(\mu I\) commutes with the logarithm:

\[ \exp(X) = e^\mu I \cdot (I + \lambda^{-1}N) = \lambda I + N = J. \]

General invertible matrix. By Jordan canonical form, \(A = P\,\mathrm{diag}(J_1,\ldots,J_r)\,P^{-1}\) with each \(J_i\) having nonzero eigenvalue. Choose \(X_i\) with \(\exp(X_i) = J_i\). Then

\[ \exp\!\left(P\,\mathrm{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_r)\,P^{-1}\right) = P\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{X_1},\ldots,e^{X_r})\,P^{-1} = A. \]
KEY RESULT
Over \(\mathbb{C}\), \(\exp: M_n(\mathbb{C}) \to GL_n(\mathbb{C})\) is surjective. Every invertible complex matrix has a logarithm. (Over \(\mathbb{R}\) this fails — Problem §1.1·7 gives a counterexample.)

§1.2 · 5 Not Every Matrix of Determinant 1 Is an Exponential of a Trace-Zero Matrix

QUESTION
Show that \(A = \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) has \(\det A = 1\) but is not \(\exp X\) for any trace-zero \(X\).
Answer

Setup. Indeed \(\det A = 1\). The formula \(\det(\exp X) = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}\) means \(\operatorname{tr}X = 0\) would give \(\det(\exp X) = 1\), consistent — so there is no determinant obstruction. The obstruction is structural.

Eigenvalue argument. Suppose \(A = \exp X\) with \(\operatorname{tr}X = 0\). Any eigenvalue \(\mu\) of \(X\) satisfies \(e^\mu = -1\), so \(\mu = (2k+1)\pi i\). With \(\operatorname{tr}X = \mu_1 + \mu_2 = 0\), we need \(\mu_2 = -\mu_1\): distinct eigenvalues \(\pm(2k+1)\pi i\). So \(X\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\), hence \(\exp X\) is also diagonalizable — but \(A\) is a non-trivial Jordan block and not diagonalizable. Contradiction.

KEY RESULT
\(\det A = 1\) is necessary but not sufficient for \(A \in \exp(\mathfrak{sl}_n)\). The matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) has determinant 1 yet is not the exponential of any trace-zero matrix, whether real or complex.

§1.2 · 6 Cayley–Hamilton Reduction of Matrix Power Series

QUESTION
Use the Cayley–Hamilton theorem to show any matrix power series \(f(X) = \sum_k a_k X^k\) can be written as \(f(X) = c_0(X)I + c_1(X)X + \cdots + c_{n-1}(X)X^{n-1}\), where each \(c_j\) is conjugation-invariant.
Answer

Reduction. By Cayley–Hamilton, \(X^n + s_{n-1}(X)X^{n-1} + \cdots + s_0(X)I = 0\), so \(X^n\) is a linear combination of \(I, X, \ldots, X^{n-1}\). Inductively, every \(X^k\) for \(k \ge n\) reduces modulo the characteristic polynomial to a combination of \(\{I, X, \ldots, X^{n-1}\}\). Applying this to each term of \(f(X) = \sum_k a_k X^k\):

\[ f(X) = c_0(X)\,I + c_1(X)\,X + \cdots + c_{n-1}(X)\,X^{n-1}. \]

Conjugation invariance. The characteristic polynomial satisfies \(\chi_{aXa^{-1}}(t) = \chi_X(t)\) for all invertible \(a\). Therefore \(s_j(aXa^{-1}) = s_j(X)\), and the coefficients \(c_j\), being power series in the \(s_j\), also satisfy \(c_j(aXa^{-1}) = c_j(X)\).

KEY RESULT
Any convergent matrix power series \(f(X)\) can be expressed as a polynomial of degree at most \(n-1\) in \(X\) with conjugation-invariant scalar coefficients depending on the eigenvalues of \(X\). This is why \(\exp(X)\), \(\sin(X)\), and similar functions always have explicit closed forms in low dimensions.

§1.2 · 7 Small Norm Condition: exp(X)v = v ⟺ Xv = 0

QUESTION
Suppose \(\|X\| < 2\pi\). Show that \(\exp(X)v = v\) if and only if \(Xv = 0\).
Answer

(\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(Xv = 0\) then \(X^kv = 0\) for all \(k \ge 1\), so \(\exp(X)v = Iv = v\). This direction requires no norm condition.

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(\exp(X)v = v\), so \((\exp X - I)v = 0\). The function \(g(z) = z/(e^z-1)\) has power series converging for \(|z| < 2\pi\). Since \(\|X\| < 2\pi\), the matrix \(g(X)\) is well-defined and satisfies \(g(X)(e^X - I) = X\). Applying to \(v\):

\[ Xv = g(X)(\exp X - I)v = g(X) \cdot 0 = 0. \]

Geometric interpretation. When \(X\) is small, no eigenvalue of \(X\) can be a nonzero multiple of \(2\pi i\), so \(\exp(X)\) has no \(2\pi\)-periodic rotation that could accidentally bring a moving vector back to itself.

KEY RESULT
For \(\|X\| < 2\pi\): \(\exp(X)v = v \iff Xv = 0.\) The radius \(2\pi\) is sharp — beyond it, rotations by \(2\pi\) can fix vectors without them being in the kernel. The key tool is the convergent series for \(z/(e^z-1)\).

§1.2 · 8 The Jacobi Identity and Lie Bracket Derivations

QUESTION
Prove \([[X,Y],Z] + [[Z,X],Y] + [[Y,Z],X] = 0\), and deduce: (a) \(\operatorname{ad}(Z)\) acts as a derivation of \([\cdot,\cdot]\); (b) \(\operatorname{ad}([X,Y]) = [\operatorname{ad}X, \operatorname{ad}Y]\).
Answer

Proof of Jacobi identity. Recall \([X,Y] = XY - YX\). Expand all three brackets and add:

\[ [[X,Y],Z] = XYZ - YXZ - ZXY + ZYX, \] \[ [[Z,X],Y] = ZXY - XZY - YZX + YXZ, \] \[ [[Y,Z],X] = YZX - ZYX - XYZ + XZY. \]

Each of the 12 terms \(\pm PQR\) (a signed permutation of \(X,Y,Z\)) appears exactly twice with opposite signs. Therefore the sum is zero.

Deduction (a) — \(\operatorname{ad}(Z)\) is a derivation. Rewrite the Jacobi identity with \((\operatorname{ad}Z)W = [Z,W]\):

\[ (\operatorname{ad}Z)[X,Y] = [Z,[X,Y]] = [[Z,X],Y] + [X,[Z,Y]] = [(\operatorname{ad}Z)X, Y] + [X, (\operatorname{ad}Z)Y]. \]

This is the Leibniz rule for \(\operatorname{ad}(Z)\) acting on the bracket product — \(\operatorname{ad}(Z)\) is a derivation of the Lie algebra.

Deduction (b) — \(\operatorname{ad}\) is a Lie algebra homomorphism. For any \(Z\):

\[ [\operatorname{ad}X, \operatorname{ad}Y](Z) = [X,[Y,Z]] - [Y,[X,Z]] = [[X,Y],Z] = \operatorname{ad}([X,Y])(Z). \]
KEY RESULT
\([[X,Y],Z]+[[Z,X],Y]+[[Y,Z],X]=0\) (Jacobi identity). This makes \(M_n\) a Lie algebra. It implies \(\operatorname{ad}: M_n \to \operatorname{End}(M_n)\) is a Lie algebra homomorphism: \(\operatorname{ad}[X,Y] = [\operatorname{ad}X, \operatorname{ad}Y]\).

§1.2 · 9 Euler's Limit Formula for the Exponential

QUESTION
Show that \(\exp X = \lim_{k\to\infty}(I + X/k)^k\).
Answer

Proof. For large \(k\), \(I + X/k\) is near the identity. The matrix logarithm satisfies

\[ \log\!\left(I + \frac{X}{k}\right) = \frac{X}{k} - \frac{X^2}{2k^2} + \frac{X^3}{3k^3} - \cdots \]

Multiplying by \(k\):

\[ k\log\!\left(I + \frac{X}{k}\right) = X - \frac{X^2}{2k} + \frac{X^3}{3k^2} - \cdots \;\xrightarrow{k\to\infty}\; X. \]

Since \(\exp\) is continuous,

\[ \left(I + \frac{X}{k}\right)^k = \exp\!\left(k\log\!\left(I+\frac{X}{k}\right)\right) \;\xrightarrow{k\to\infty}\; \exp(X). \]

Interpretation. Taking \(k\) many small linear steps \(I + X/k\) — each step approximately "flowing by \(X\) for time \(1/k\)" — converges to the continuous flow \(\exp(X)\) as \(k \to \infty\).

KEY RESULT
\(\exp X = \lim_{k\to\infty}(I + X/k)^k.\) This matrix analogue of Euler's compound interest formula is fundamental: it defines \(\exp\) via iterated linear approximation and provides the basis for the Trotter product formula.

§1.2 · 10 The Trotter Product Formula

QUESTION
Prove: \(\exp(X+Y) = \lim_{k\to\infty}\bigl(\exp(X/k)\,\exp(Y/k)\bigr)^k.\)
Answer

Proof. For small \(t = 1/k\), expand each factor:

\[ \exp(tX)\exp(tY) = (I + tX + O(t^2))(I + tY + O(t^2)) = I + t(X+Y) + O(t^2). \]

Comparing with \(\exp(t(X+Y)) = I + t(X+Y) + O(t^2)\), we see \(\exp(tX)\exp(tY) = \exp(t(X+Y)+O(t^2))\). Setting \(t = 1/k\) and using Problem 9:

\[ \left(\exp\frac{X}{k}\exp\frac{Y}{k}\right)^k = \left(I + \frac{X+Y}{k} + O(k^{-2})\right)^k \;\xrightarrow{k\to\infty}\; \exp(X+Y). \]
KEY RESULT — TROTTER PRODUCT FORMULA
\[\exp(X+Y) = \lim_{k\to\infty}\!\left(\exp\!\tfrac{X}{k}\exp\!\tfrac{Y}{k}\right)^k.\] This holds even when \(X\) and \(Y\) do not commute. It is fundamental in quantum mechanics (splitting Hamiltonians), numerical ODE solvers (operator splitting), and functional analysis.

§1.2 · 11 Continuous One-Parameter Matrix Groups

QUESTION
Let \(a: \mathbb{R} \to M\) be continuous with \(a(\sigma+\tau) = a(\sigma)a(\tau)\) and \(a(0) = I\). Show \(a(\tau) = \exp(\tau X)\) for some \(X \in M\).
Answer

Local form. Since \(a\) is continuous and \(a(0) = I\), for sufficiently small \(\tau\) we have \(a(\tau)\) near \(I\), so \(\log a(\tau)\) is defined. Call \(X(\tau) = \log a(\tau)\). The functional equation implies all \(a(\tau)\) commute (since both sides equal \(a(\sigma+\tau) = a(\tau+\sigma)\)). Therefore for small \(\sigma, \tau\):

\[ X(\sigma+\tau) = \log a(\sigma+\tau) = \log(a(\sigma)a(\tau)) = \log a(\sigma) + \log a(\tau) = X(\sigma) + X(\tau). \]

A continuous additive function satisfies \(X(\tau) = \tau X\) for a fixed matrix \(X = X(1)\). Thus \(a(\tau) = \exp(\tau X)\) for small \(\tau\).

Extension. For general \(\tau\), choose integer \(m\) with \(\tau/m\) small. Then

\[ a(\tau) = a(\tau/m)^m = \exp\!\left(\frac{\tau}{m}X\right)^m = \exp(\tau X). \]
KEY RESULT
Every continuous one-parameter matrix group is of the form \(a(\tau) = \exp(\tau X)\). Continuity alone (no differentiability assumed) forces this form. This is the matrix version of the classification of one-dimensional Lie groups.

§1.2 · 12 Invariant Subspaces Under the Adjoint Action

QUESTION
Let \([X,L] \subset L\) for a subspace \(L \subset M\). Show: (a) \(\exp(\tau X)\,L\,\exp(-\tau X) \subset L\). (b) If also \(L \cdot L \subset L\), then \(\exp(-X)\exp(X+L) \subset I+L\).
Answer

Part (a). For \(Y \in L\), define \(F(\tau) = \exp(\tau X)\,Y\,\exp(-\tau X)\). Differentiating:

\[ F'(\tau) = [X, F(\tau)]. \]

Since \(F(0) = Y \in L\) and \([X,L] \subset L\), the differential equation \(F' = [X,F]\) with initial value in \(L\) stays in \(L\). More explicitly:

\[ F(\tau) = e^{\tau\operatorname{ad}X}Y = Y + \tau[X,Y] + \frac{\tau^2}{2!}[X,[X,Y]] + \cdots \in L. \]

Part (b). Let \(Y \in L\), and define \(a(t) = \exp(-tX)\exp(t(X+Y))\). Then \(a(0) = I\) and

\[ a'(t) = \exp(-tX)\,Y\,\exp(t(X+Y)) = \underbrace{\exp(-tX)\,Y\,\exp(tX)}_{\in L \text{ by (a)}}\cdot a(t). \]

Since \(LL \subset L\), integrating from 0 to 1 gives \(a(1) - I \in L\), so \(\exp(-X)\exp(X+Y) \in I+L\).

KEY RESULT
If a subspace \(L\) is invariant under \(\operatorname{ad}(X)\) (i.e., \([X,L] \subset L\)), then \(L\) is invariant under the adjoint action of the one-parameter group \(\exp(\tau X)\). This is the infinitesimal-to-global principle for Lie algebra ideals.

§1.2 · 13 Jacobi's Formula — Derivative of the Determinant

QUESTION
Show that for any differentiable invertible matrix-valued function \(a(\tau)\): \[\dfrac{d}{d\tau}\det a = (\det a)\,\operatorname{tr}\!\left(a^{-1}\dfrac{da}{d\tau}\right).\]
Answer

Step 1 — Identity case. Suppose \(a(0) = I\), write \(a(\tau) = I + \tau B + o(\tau)\) with \(B = a'(0)\). Then

\[ \det(I + \tau B + o(\tau)) = 1 + \tau\operatorname{tr}B + o(\tau). \]

Differentiating at \(\tau = 0\):

\[ \left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\det a\right|_{\tau=0} = \operatorname{tr}(a'(0)) = \operatorname{tr}\!\left(a^{-1}\frac{da}{d\tau}\right)\bigg|_{\tau=0}. \]

Step 2 — General case. For general invertible \(a(\tau_0)\), let \(b(h) = a(\tau_0)^{-1}a(\tau_0+h)\). Then \(b(0) = I\) and \(b'(0) = a(\tau_0)^{-1}a'(\tau_0)\). Using \(\det a(\tau_0+h) = \det a(\tau_0)\cdot\det b(h)\) and Step 1:

\[ \frac{d}{d\tau}\det a(\tau_0) = \det a(\tau_0)\cdot\operatorname{tr}\bigl(b'(0)\bigr) = \det a(\tau_0)\cdot\operatorname{tr}\!\left(a(\tau_0)^{-1}a'(\tau_0)\right). \]

Corollary. Setting \(a(\tau) = \exp(\tau X)\):

\[ \frac{d}{d\tau}\det\exp(\tau X) = \det\exp(\tau X)\cdot\operatorname{tr}(X) \implies \det\exp(X) = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}. \]
KEY RESULT — JACOBI'S FORMULA
\[\frac{d}{d\tau}\det a = (\det a)\,\operatorname{tr}\!\left(a^{-1}\frac{da}{d\tau}\right),\quad\text{equivalently, }\; d(\log\det a) = \operatorname{tr}(a^{-1}\,da).\] The corollary \(\det(\exp X) = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}\) connects the determinant (a multiplicative invariant) to the trace (an additive invariant) via the exponential.

Summary of Main Ideas

The Central Correspondence The matrix exponential converts infinitesimal generators into finite transformations: \(\,Xp\;\longrightarrow\;\gamma_p(t)=\exp(tX)p.\) Every concept in §1.1–1.2 is a variation on this theme.
Geometry from Algebra Skew-symmetric \(X\) generates orthogonal flows. Cross-product fields generate 3D rotations (Rodrigues). Nilpotent \(X\) generates polynomial translations. The exponential turns algebraic properties of \(X\) into geometric properties of the flow.
Bijections and Decompositions \(\exp\) maps: nilpotent \(\leftrightarrow\) unipotent; semisimple \(\to\) semisimple; additive Jordan \(\to\) multiplicative Jordan. Over \(\mathbb{C}\), \(\exp\) is surjective onto invertible matrices. Over \(\mathbb{R}\), it is not.
Limit Formulas and the Lie Bracket \(\exp(X) = \lim(I+X/k)^k\) (Euler). \(\exp(X+Y) = \lim(\exp(X/k)\exp(Y/k))^k\) (Trotter, valid even without commutativity). The Jacobi identity \([[X,Y],Z]+\text{cyclic}=0\) makes \(M_n\) a Lie algebra. The formula \(\det\exp X = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}\) links all invariants.
